content:
Earlier this year, Apple decided to discontinue the Pro Display XDR entirely. Despite its impressive hardware, the monitor had not been updated for years and still retails for over US$6,000. Apple's new display lineup now consists of the Studio Display and the brand-new Studio Display XDR. While each has its own highlights, both are currently only available with a 27-inch 5K screen. The XDR starts at a hefty US$3,299, and with upgrades, it can reach US$3,600 before tax. This has left a gap in the market for other manufacturers to offer larger-sized Retina-class displays for Mac users — and that's exactly where the brand-new Meirro Pro comes in. The Meirro Pro is a 32-inch 6K display built with a full aluminum chassis, supports single-cable connection, and comes with an adjustable stand — all for just US$1,199. I've been using it as my primary monitor, and although Meirro has made a few compromises to keep the price down, it may well be the most compelling Studio Display alternative I've tested. Here's everything you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video of the Meirro Pro for a closer look at this product!

Design and Specifications

The first thing that stands out is how remarkably similar it looks to the current Apple Studio Display. This monitor fits naturally into any Apple-styled desk setup. It's crafted from fully CNC-machined aluminum and comes with an adjustable stand made of the same material, giving it an exceptionally premium feel. The build quality inspires confidence throughout your entire setup. Most non-Apple displays on the market use plastic enclosures with stands that often feel flimsy — but the Meirro Pro uses absolutely no plastic anywhere on the device.

Unboxing and setup are also refreshingly straightforward. Simply attach the base to the stand, secure the stand to the back of the display, plug in the power, and it's ready to go. The design is extremely minimalist, with no buttons at all, and most importantly, the power supply is built into the monitor. This means there's no bulky external power brick dangling from the cable, keeping your desk setup wonderfully clean. Both the adjustable stand and VESA mount are included in the box at no extra cost. So yes, this is a product heavily inspired by Apple's design language — and it absolutely delivers on my expectations.

But how does it actually perform in terms of display quality? As I mentioned at the start, this is a true 6K panel. It uses a 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel with a resolution of 6144 × 3456, which works out to 224 ppi — delivering true Retina-level sharpness. Here are the key specifications:

  • 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel
  • 6144 × 3456 resolution
  • 224 PPI
  • 60Hz refresh rate
  • 2,000:1 contrast ratio
  • 10-bit color supporting over 1.07 billion colors
  • 98% DCI-P3 color gamut
  • 99.5% Adobe RGB color gamut
  • Typical brightness of 450 nits, HDR peak brightness of 750 nits

The panel is only available with a glossy anti-reflective coating as the sole option. While I would have liked a matte coating as an alternative, even in a brightly lit room with plenty of windows, the glossy coating still performs admirably.

Ports and Accessories

Similar to Apple's display offerings, the Meirro Pro keeps its port selection minimal — the back features only five USB-C ports for all I/O. One of these serves as the primary upstream connection, supporting DisplayPort 2.1 with bandwidth up to 80Gbps, and can deliver up to 96W of power passthrough to keep your MacBook charged at all times. This means a single cable handles the entire 6K video signal. The remaining four USB-C ports are downstream ports with limited data transfer speeds — all at USB 2.0 specification. However, they're more than adequate for connecting webcams, speakers, and other peripherals.

Since the Meirro Pro has no buttons whatsoever (not even a power button), a remote control closely resembling the previous-generation Apple TV remote is included in the box. This remote features a power button and provides access to the display's system settings when needed.

My Experience and Setup

I've had the Meirro Pro set up as the sole primary display on my desk, and the experience has been outstanding. The 32-inch screen size combined with 6K resolution satisfies all my expectations for a high-end Mac monitor — both in terms of physical real estate and pixel density.

My setup is quite simple. I personally use multiple external SSDs and prefer the Satechi Thunderbolt hub, so I connect the display through that hub. One Thunderbolt cable runs from the display to the hub, and another Thunderbolt cable runs from the hub to my MacBook Pro. Everything works exactly as expected.

I've tested this display across all my daily workflows, and it handles them with ease. Working in Final Cut Pro — including editing timelines and organizing media files — the extra screen space has been a tremendous help. A large part of my daily work involves research, requiring numerous tabs and windows open simultaneously; the higher pixel density makes the screen feel even larger than its actual 32-inch size. The most important feature of this display is its 224 PPI, which allows macOS — and even iPadOS — to scale exactly as Apple intended.

One last thing worth mentioning is that the solid build quality helps reduce monitor wobble. Most displays on the market shake when you type at your desk, and this becomes especially noticeable with a sit-stand desk like mine. The combination of premium materials and a sturdy stand effectively minimizes this wobble. So, whether judged by specs or real-world use, the Meirro Pro has every reason to serve as a Studio Display alternative. However, at this price point, there are some compromises worth addressing.

The Compromises

I'll say it again — a 32-inch 6K display with CNC aluminum construction for under US$1,200 sounds almost too good to be true. Meirro had to make some tough decisions to bring the price down to this level. Since most potential buyers will compare it to the Studio Display, it's important to point out the features it lacks. The Meirro Pro does not include or support:

  • Built-in webcam
  • Speakers
  • Microphone
  • No daisy-chaining support

Personally, these compromises are well worth the savings, since I already own external webcams and speakers. The lack of a microphone doesn't affect me much either, as I use AirPods or a Shure microphone when needed. Still, I want to highlight these details so prospective buyers have a clearer picture.

The final compromise I noticed concerns the speed of the USB-C ports on the back of the display. The Apple Studio Display offers a total of four USB-C ports — two of which are Thunderbolt, and the other two at USB 3.0 speeds. The Meirro Pro offers more USB-C ports overall, but only one is Thunderbolt, while the remaining four are the slower USB 2.0 specification. For me, this isn't a major issue because I have the Satechi Thunderbolt dock; however, I understand that some users may need faster ports.

Even taking these compromises into account, I still believe the Meirro Pro is an unequivocal recommendation over the Apple Studio Display, because the value it offers is simply too high.

Price and Availability

The Meirro Pro is priced at US$1,299 as standard, and is currently available for pre-order at US$1,199. Shipping is expected to begin on August 1st. If you already have a monitor arm, you can opt out of the included stand to save US$50, bringing the total down to US$1,149. The US$1,199 price includes:

  • Meirro Pro display
  • Aluminum stand
  • VESA mount
  • USB-C cable
  • Power cable
  • Remote control

Conclusion

The Meirro Pro is the best true Studio Display alternative I've ever tested. For just US$1,199, you get a 32-inch 6K display with Retina-level sharpness, a glossy Nano IPS Black panel, a full aluminum body, single-cable Mac connectivity, an adjustable stand, and a VESA mount. If you're after Apple's most complete all-in-one desktop experience, the Studio Display still has its merits; but if you already own some external accessories and truly value screen size, resolution, build quality, and value for money, the Meirro Pro is an absolutely worthwhile recommendation.

What do you think? Would you consider this display? Do you already own a Studio Display? Do you miss the Pro Display XDR? I'd love to hear your thoughts. And remember — be sure to watch our video to experience its real-world performance firsthand!
